newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sluggish Japan spending to keep brake on economy.
newsitem.headline: Sluggish Japan spending to keep brake on economy.

text.p: Japanese consumers worried about their job and salary prospects are keeping a tight rein on spending and there seems little chance of them going on an economy-boosting buying spree, analysts say.

Despite a year of rockbottom interest rates, consumer spending is still sluggish, held back by concerns generated by the fragile state of the economy, which is in turn putting a drag on recovery, they say.

Both the Bank of Japan (BOJ) and the government have said a rise in private spending is one of the keys to a full-fledged recovery. But consumer confidence is proving slow to pick up as salaried workers who can no longer rely on a system of lifetime employment fret about future job and income prospects.
"The minds of consumers are bleaker than the actual state of the economy," said Osamu Kubotani, senior analyst at NLI Research Institute.
Other economists agreed that consumption was not likely to pick up in the short-term, given job and income concerns.

Although unemployment rates are not rising, there is no real sign of major improvement either. Japan's jobless rate fell to 3.3 percent in August from 3.4 percent in July. But the government said there was still cause for concern, citing a rise in unemployment among middle-aged and older workers due to aggressive corporate restructuring and cost-cutting.
NLI's Kubotani also said consumers were aware that companies were looking to cut costs further, creating a climate of insecurity. "After all, most consumers are employees of corporations," he said.
Sales at department stores posted a modest year-on-year rise of 1.2 percent in August while sales at Japanese chain stores fell 0.2 percent from a year earlier.

Wages have also been static. The average annual salary of workers employed by the private sector increased in 1995, but only by a mere 0.4 percent from a year ago. The average salary was 4.57 million yen ($40,800), and the sluggish growth is largely due to a 1.6 percent drop in bonuses, economists said.
Many Japanese use their hefty, twice yearly bonuses for big purchases such as cars and computers.
An official at the government's Economic Planning Agency (EPA) also said there was a disparity in income trends between employees of big and small companies.

"While the income of employees of larger firms shows signs of picking up, those (salaries) at small and medium-sized firms are still heading nowhere," said Yoshiaki Takebayashi, an official at the EPA's research bureau.
Takebayashi said that once consumers feel confident about the outlook for salaries, consumption will pick up.
Kubotani also said strong housing sales was a sign that the potential is there.
Japan's housing starts in August rose 14.3 percent from a year earlier to 135,748 units, and those for condominiums were particularly strong, rising by 25.1 percent to 15,443 units.
Economists said one of the reasons was the so-called "rush-in" demand ahead of a planned rise in the consumption tax to take place next April, as well as low interest rates.
The key discount rate has been at a record low 0.5 percent for just over a year to help the economy pull out of the slump that followed the collapse of the 1980s "bubble" economy.

"Just as the planned tax rise provided an incentive to buy houses, we need a trigger to turn potential demand into actual spending. Many consumers are just putting off spending. An optimistic view on income could change that," Kubotani said.
